title: Pan and zoom
description: Pan and zoom are the canvas's fundamental verbs: translate the viewport, scale around the cursor. The math is a 2D transform (scale + offset); the feel is in the details — zoom-to-cursor (not to center), smooth interpolation, and sane limits (min/max zoom). Get the transform right once and every feature (selection, minimap, export) builds on it.
mechanism: View transform: screen = world * scale + offset. Zoom at cursor: adjust offset so the world point under the cursor stays put. Clamp scale; interpolate for smoothness.
algo: O(1) transform per frame; all rendering through it.
demo:
# zoom-to-cursor: the world point under the cursor stays put
scale, ox = 1.0, 0.0

def zoom_at(cursor_x, factor):
    global scale, ox
    world_x = (cursor_x - ox) / scale   # world point under cursor
    scale *= factor
    ox = cursor_x - world_x * scale     # keep it under the cursor

print('scale=%.1f offset=%.1f' % (scale, ox))
zoom_at(100, 2.0)
print('after 2x zoom at x=100: scale=%.1f offset=%.1f' % (scale, ox))
print('world point under cursor unchanged: no disorienting jump')

title: Virtualized rendering
description: An infinite canvas holds millions of objects but the screen shows hundreds: virtualized rendering draws only the viewport (plus a margin). A spatial index answers 'what is visible?' per frame; everything else is skipped. The margin prefetches during pans so fast scrolling never shows blank tiles. Without virtualization, the canvas dies at thousands of objects; with it, millions are routine.
mechanism: Spatial index (quadtree/R-tree) query per frame for the viewport rect; draw those; prefetch margin tiles. Object count on screen bounded by pixels, not by data.
algo: Spatial index query per frame for the viewport rect; draw only hits plus a prefetch margin.
demo:
import random
random.seed(1)
# 1M objects in the world; viewport shows a tiny rect
objs = [(random.uniform(0, 10000), random.uniform(0, 10000)) for _ in range(100000)]
viewport = (100, 100, 400, 300)  # x, y, w, h

def visible(objs, vp):
    x, y, w, h = vp
    return [o for o in objs if x <= o[0] <= x + w and y <= o[1] <= y + h]

vis = visible(objs, viewport)
print('world objects: %d | drawn this frame: %d' % (len(objs), len(vis)))
print('per-frame cost ~ O(visible), not O(world): millions are routine')
print('(production uses a quadtree, not a scan -- same idea, faster query)')

title: Canvas vs SVG vs WebGL
description: The renderer choice shapes the canvas: SVG gives DOM nodes per object (great interop, dies past ~10k nodes), Canvas 2D draws immediate-mode (fast to 100k, manual hit-testing), WebGL batches everything on the GPU (millions, most work). The rule from the DOM-size work: keep DOM nodes bounded — Canvas/WebGL for the objects, DOM only for the UI chrome.
mechanism: SVG: node per object. Canvas: draw calls per frame, spatial index for hit-testing. WebGL: instanced batches, shaders for styles. Hybrid: WebGL for objects, DOM for selected/editing.
algo: SVG O(nodes) DOM; Canvas O(visible) draws; WebGL O(visible) batched.
demo:
scales = [
    ('SVG (DOM/node)', 10_000, 'interop, dies past ~10k nodes'),
    ('Canvas 2D', 100_000, 'fast draws, manual hit-testing'),
    ('WebGL', 10_000_000, 'GPU batches, most engineering'),
]
print('%-16s %10s  %s' % ('renderer', 'objects', 'notes'))
for name, n, note in scales:
    print('%-16s %10d  %s' % (name, n, note))
print('rule: DOM nodes bounded; canvas/WebGL for objects, DOM for UI chrome')

title: Spatial indexes for canvas
description: Every frame asks 'what is in this rect?' — the spatial index answers. Quadtrees subdivide uniformly (simple, good for even distributions); R-trees pack by object bounds (better for varied sizes, the database choice). The index is rebuilt or updated incrementally as objects move; queries are O(log n + hits). It is the same structure as the database's geospatial index, applied to pixels.
mechanism: Insert object bounds; query rect returns candidates; exact hit-test on candidates. Incremental updates on move; rebuild when the distribution shifts badly.
algo: O(log n + hits) query; O(log n) update.

title: Level of detail (LOD)
description: Level of detail renders distant objects cheaply: a node is a dot at zoom 0.1, a box at 1x, full detail at 10x. LOD keeps frame rates constant as you zoom out over millions of objects — the alternative is drawing full detail for pixels nobody can see. Thresholds per zoom level; crossfade to avoid popping. Maps have done this forever (countries -> cities -> streets).
mechanism: Per object type: detail thresholds by zoom; render the appropriate representation. Aggregate: at far zoom, draw clusters not individuals. Precompute simplified geometries per level.
algo: O(visible) with cheaper per-object cost at far zoom; aggregation O(clusters).

title: Minimap
description: The minimap is the canvas in miniature: whole-world overview, viewport rectangle, click/drag to navigate. It renders from the same scene at tiny scale (LOD: dots), updates on change, and the viewport rect is draggable. It solves 'where am I' on infinite canvases — without it, users get lost in whitespace.
mechanism: Render scene bounds to a small offscreen canvas (dots/clusters); overlay the viewport rect; interactions on the minimap move the main viewport. Update on scene change (debounced).
algo: O(scene) to render the minimap, debounced; O(1) interactions.
demo:
# minimap: world -> tiny rect; viewport rect draggable
WORLD = (0, 0, 10000, 10000)
MINI = 120  # px
viewport = (1000, 2000, 800, 600)

def to_mini(x, y):
    sx = MINI / WORLD[2]
    return (x * sx, y * sx)

vx, vy = to_mini(viewport[0], viewport[1])
vw, vh = viewport[2] * MINI / WORLD[2], viewport[3] * MINI / WORLD[3]
print('minimap %dpx: viewport rect at (%.1f, %.1f) size %.1fx%.1f' % (MINI, vx, vy, vw, vh))
print('click/drag the rect: main viewport follows ("where am I" solved)')

title: Clustering on canvas
description: At far zoom, individual objects merge into clusters: '1.2k nodes' as one dot, expanding as you zoom in. Clustering runs on the spatial index (grid or k-means per viewport) and updates per frame-cheaply. It is LOD for dense data — the alternative is overdraw soup. Click a cluster to zoom into it: the interaction writes itself.
mechanism: Grid-cluster per viewport at far zoom (cell size ~ pixels); label with counts; on zoom-in past threshold, switch to individuals. Incremental: only recluster on viewport/data change.
algo: O(visible) grid clustering per viewport change.
demo:
# grid clustering: one dot per cell at far zoom, with counts
import random
random.seed(3)
pts = [(random.uniform(0, 100), random.uniform(0, 100)) for _ in range(5000)]
CELL = 10

from collections import Counter
cells = Counter((int(x // CELL), int(y // CELL)) for x, y in pts)
print('5000 points -> %d cluster dots at far zoom' % len(cells))
big = cells.most_common(3)
print('largest clusters:', [(c, '%d pts' % n) for c, n in big])
print('click a cluster -> zoom in -> individuals appear')

title: Force-directed layouts
description: Force-directed layouts position graph nodes by simulation: repulsion between all pairs, attraction along edges, iterate to equilibrium. The result reveals clusters and hubs organically. It is O(n^2) naive — Barnes-Hut approximation (quadtree) makes it O(n log n) — and it runs incrementally as the graph changes. Layout is presentation, not data: store positions, recompute on demand.
mechanism: Forces: repulsion (Coulomb-like), attraction (springs on edges), centering gravity. Integrate with cooling (decreasing step). Barnes-Hut via the spatial index for scale.
algo: O(n^2) naive; O(n log n) Barnes-Hut. Iterative to equilibrium.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(7)
# tiny force layout: 6 nodes, ring + hub edges
nodes = {i: [random.uniform(-1, 1), random.uniform(-1, 1)] for i in range(6)}
edges = [(0, i) for i in range(1, 6)] + [(1, 2), (2, 3)]

for _ in range(50):  # iterate to equilibrium
    F = {i: [0.0, 0.0] for i in nodes}
    for i in nodes:
        for j in nodes:
            if i >= j:
                continue
            dx, dy = nodes[i][0] - nodes[j][0], nodes[i][1] - nodes[j][1]
            d = max(0.1, math.hypot(dx, dy))
            f = 0.01 / (d * d)  # repulsion
            F[i][0] += f * dx / d; F[i][1] += f * dy / d
            F[j][0] -= f * dx / d; F[j][1] -= f * dy / d
    for a, b in edges:  # springs on edges
        dx, dy = nodes[b][0] - nodes[a][0], nodes[b][1] - nodes[a][1]
        d = max(0.1, math.hypot(dx, dy))
        f = 0.05 * (d - 1.0)
        F[a][0] += f * dx / d; F[a][1] += f * dy / d
        F[b][0] -= f * dx / d; F[b][1] -= f * dy / d
    for i in nodes:
        nodes[i][0] += F[i][0]; nodes[i][1] += F[i][1]

for i, (x, y) in sorted(nodes.items()):
    print('node %d: (%6.2f, %6.2f)' % (i, x, y))
print('hub (0) centered, ring spread: structure revealed by simulation')

title: Hit testing
description: Hit testing answers 'what is under the cursor?' — via the spatial index for candidates, then exact geometry (point-in-shape) on the few. Z-order matters: test topmost first. For Canvas/WebGL (no DOM), hit-testing is manual but fast; for SVG it is free (the browser does it). The pattern is broad-phase (index) then narrow-phase (geometry), same as physics engines.
mechanism: Broad: spatial index query at the point. Narrow: point-in-rect/circle/path per candidate, topmost first. Return the topmost hit + the stack for marquee/modifier selection.
algo: O(log n + candidates) broad; O(candidates) narrow.
demo:
# broad-phase (spatial) then narrow-phase (geometry), topmost first
shapes = [
    {'id': 'a', 'z': 1, 'rect': (0, 0, 10, 10)},
    {'id': 'b', 'z': 2, 'rect': (5, 5, 10, 10)},  # on top of a
]

def hit(x, y):
    cands = [s for s in shapes  # broad: bbox check
             if s['rect'][0] <= x <= s['rect'][0] + s['rect'][2]
             and s['rect'][1] <= y <= s['rect'][1] + s['rect'][3]]
    cands.sort(key=lambda s: -s['z'])  # topmost first
    return cands[0]['id'] if cands else None

print('click (7,7):', hit(7, 7), '(b: topmost of the two overlapping)')
print('click (2,2):', hit(2, 2))
print('click (99,99):', hit(99, 99))

title: Collaboration cursors
description: Multiplayer cursors show where collaborators are: each user's viewport and cursor broadcast at ~10Hz, rendered as colored carets with name flags. The data layer is CRDTs or OT for the shared document; cursors are ephemeral presence (no persistence needed). The UX details matter most: colors per user, 'follow' mode, and not rendering your own cursor back at you.
mechanism: Presence channel (websocket) for viewports/cursors; CRDT for document state; render remote cursors as overlays. Throttle broadcasts; interpolate movement for smoothness.
algo: O(users) overlays; presence O(1) per broadcast.

title: Canvas persistence
description: Infinite canvases persist as document models (objects + positions), not pixels: the save format is JSON/CRDT ops, versioned, with incremental sync. Large canvases page the model (load visible regions first, stream the rest). Undo is a first-class citizen — command stack or CRDT history — because canvas editing is exploratory. Export renders the model to SVG/PNG/PDF on demand.
mechanism: Document model with schema version; incremental save (dirty regions); CRDT for collaboration; undo stack of inverse ops. Export: render model at requested scale.
demo:
import json

# document model: objects + schema version (not pixels)
doc = {'v': 3, 'objects': [
    {'id': 'a', 'type': 'rect', 'x': 10, 'y': 20, 'w': 100, 'h': 50},
    {'id': 'b', 'type': 'text', 'x': 30, 'y': 40, 'text': 'hello'},
]}
blob = json.dumps(doc)
print('saved %d bytes (model, versioned)' % len(blob))
# migrate v2 -> v3 on load
print('load: check v, migrate if old, stream visible regions first')
print('undo: inverse ops on the model (exploratory editing needs it)')

title: Canvas performance budgets
description: Canvas performance is budgeted per frame: 16ms for 60fps, split across input, query, draw, and composite. The budgets force the architecture — virtualization, LOD, batching — and the frame profiler shows which link breaks. Common killers: per-object DOM nodes, unbatched draw calls, and layout thrash from reading DOM geometry in the draw loop. Budget first, optimize second.
mechanism: Frame budget 16ms; instrument per phase; alert on overruns. Rules: no per-object DOM, batch draws, never read layout in the draw loop. Profile on the slowest supported device.
algo: O(1) instrumentation per frame; the budgets drive design.
demo:
budget = {'input': 2, 'spatial-query': 3, 'draw': 8, 'composite': 3}  # ms, total 16
measured = {'input': 1, 'spatial-query': 2, 'draw': 14, 'composite': 2}

print('phase           budget  actual')
for phase, b in budget.items():
    m = measured[phase]
    print('%-15s %4dms  %4dms %s' % (phase, b, m, '<- OVER' if m > b else ''))
print('draw over budget: batch the draw calls (killers: per-object DOM, layout thrash)')

title: Canvas accessibility
description: Canvases are famously hostile to assistive tech — pixels have no semantics. The fixes: a DOM fallback (list view of the objects, fully keyboard-operable), text alternatives per object, keyboard pan/zoom (arrows, +/-), and sonification where useful. The canvas is the visual view; the list is the accessible view; both edit the same model. 'Canvas with no alternative' fails WCAG.
mechanism: Parallel DOM list mirroring the model; keyboard shortcuts for pan/zoom/select; ARIA descriptions per object; focus visible on the canvas container. Same model, two views.
algo: O(objects) list render, virtualized; the model is shared.
demo:
objects = [{'id': 'a', 'type': 'rect', 'label': 'Revenue chart, Q1-Q4'}, {'id': 'b', 'type': 'text', 'label': 'Note: review Friday'}]
print('ACCESSIBLE LIST VIEW (mirrors the canvas model):')
for o in objects:
    print('  - [%s] %s (keyboard: arrows move, Enter selects)' % (o['type'], o['label']))
print('canvas: arrows pan, +/- zoom; every object has a text alternative')
print('same model, two views: pixels for sight, list for assistive tech')

title: Canvas export
description: Export renders the model at any scale: SVG for vectors (infinite zoom, small files), PNG for rasters (scale factor for retina), PDF for print. The exporter walks the model — not the screen — so export resolution is independent of the viewport. Selection export, artboard export, and whole-canvas export are the three scopes; background and scale are options, not afterthoughts.
mechanism: Walk the model; emit per format; scale transform for raster. Vector export preserves editability; raster bakes pixels. Async for large canvases with progress.
demo:
# export walks the MODEL (not the screen): resolution independent of viewport
model = [{'type': 'rect', 'x': 10, 'y': 20, 'w': 100, 'h': 50}]

def to_svg(objs, scale=1):
    parts = ['<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">']
    for o in objs:
        parts.append('<rect x="%d" y="%d" width="%d" height="%d"/>' %
                     (o['x'] * scale, o['y'] * scale, o['w'] * scale, o['h'] * scale))
    return ''.join(parts) + '</svg>'

print(to_svg(model, scale=2))
print('SVG: infinite zoom. PNG: scale factor for retina. Same model walk.')

title: Mobile canvas
description: Mobile canvases trade precision for touch: fat-finger hit targets (44pt minimum), pinch to zoom, two-finger pan, and palm rejection. Rendering budgets shrink (weaker GPUs, thermal throttling) — LOD thresholds get more aggressive, and background work pauses when the app backgrounds. The interaction model is touch-first, not mouse-shrunk: gestures replace hover, long-press replaces right-click.
mechanism: Touch gestures (pinch/pan/tap/long-press); 44pt hit targets; aggressive LOD; pause background work on suspend. No hover: every hover feature needs a touch equivalent.
algo: O(1) gesture handling; LOD more aggressive.
demo:
# touch: pinch zoom around the midpoint, 44pt hit targets
def pinch(d0, d1, center):
    factor = d1 / d0
    return 'zoom %.2fx around %s' % (factor, center)

print(pinch(100, 150, (200, 200)))
print('hit targets >= 44pt (fat fingers); long-press = right-click')
print('no hover on touch: every hover feature needs a touch equivalent')
print('thermal throttling: LOD more aggressive, background work pauses')
